paras: The Bross hoodoo story was a December 1888 newspaper account from Kingman County, Kansas, that an elderly Black servant had tortured her employer's daughter, whom she believed had 'hoodooed' her, and that a posse was hunting the servant to lynch her. No paper reported her capture, and within days a Kansas paper dismissed the story as a lie.

According to the dispatches, farmer and cattleman Eugene Bartlett lived near the village of Bross with his children and a Black domestic servant who had been a slave. In one version the servant, called 'good old Rebecca', had come with the family from Kentucky, while a Wyoming paper said the Bartletts had come from England. All versions agree that she came to believe the elder daughter had bewitched her, and that the girl, in fun, encouraged the belief.

The first wire, a Kingman County merchant's account sent from Wichita, said that while the family was out the servant tied, stripped, beat and painted the sixteen-year-old girl, locked her in a room and fled, leaving her in critical condition. A second account attached to it from St. Louis said she had tied the girl in a fireplace and set a fire, and that the girl died during the night.

A fuller version came from George W. Beatty, a farmer near Bross, who said the attack took place on a Monday evening after the servant sent away Robert Donnelly, a young man visiting Jennie Bartlett. In his telling she hung the girl from a joist, covered her with paint and tar and lit a kettle of oiled kindling beneath her, and Donnelly returned, broke in and cut her down minutes before she died. Over twenty men then went to the house, found the servant gone along with one of the horses, and began a hunt.

The St. Louis account said the country was 'being scoured' and that the servant would be lynched if found, while the Beatty version spoke of efforts 'to effect an arrest'. Kansas papers a week later still said only that she had disappeared, and no report of her capture, an inquest or an arrest appears in the coverage.

The merchant's wire ran on December 19 and 20 in dailies from Washington and New York to Memphis, under headlines such as 'Thought She Was Hoodooed' and 'Superstition in the West'. The Memphis Appeal added a deck promising that 'A Pursuing Posse Will do Some Lynching.' The Beatty version appeared in the Omaha Daily Bee as 'Burned to Break a Spell' and in Missouri and Kansas weeklies as 'A Fiend's Crime' and 'Hoodoo Horror'.

Editorial comment treated the lynching as likely rather than objectionable: the Smyrna Times in Delaware called the servant's belief 'hoodoo rot' and predicted the lynching party would 'in all probability' succeed. In Kansas the reception was cooler, as the Barbour County Index called it a 'sensational story' and the Wichita Eagle reprinted the Topeka Journal's protest against 'Another lie' and the 'malicious circulation of lies about Kansas'.

The accounts disagree on the girl's age, sixteen or about twenty, and on whether she was beaten and survived or was burned to death. The Topeka Journal's denial gave no particulars, and the coverage contains no local Kingman County report that confirms either version.

reader.title: Bross hoodoo story and manhunt
bases: The only racial violence reported is a threatened lynching: a posse or search party hunting a Black servant accused of killing her employer's daughter, whom the wire said 'will be lynched' if found (A1, A2, A3); no capture or violence against her is reported.

Over twenty men went to the house and a hunt followed (A3, A17), and one wire predicted a lynching (A1, A2), but no paper reports the accused woman caught or killed; the last Kansas notices say she had disappeared (A16, A17).

Two Wichita versions (a merchant's and George W. Beatty's) were widely printed but disagree on whether the girl was burned and died (A1, A3, A15), and the Topeka Journal, reprinted by the Wichita Eagle, called the burning story 'Another lie' (A10).

accounts.label: Kingman County merchant (Wichita wire)
accounts.gist: The servant tied, stripped, beat and painted the sixteen-year-old daughter, locked her in a room and fled; the girl was found next morning in critical condition.

accounts.label: 'Another account' (St. Louis wire)
accounts.gist: The servant tied the painted girl in a fireplace and set a fire; a neighbor rescued her but she died in the night; the country was being scoured and the servant would be lynched if found.

accounts.label: George W. Beatty (Wichita)
accounts.gist: 'Good old Rebecca' sent Donnelly away, hung Jennie Bartlett from a joist, tarred her and lit a fire beneath her; she died minutes after Donnelly rescued her; over twenty men searched and a hunt began.

accounts.label: Platte Valley Lyre variant
accounts.gist: An English family near 'Becoss'; the girl was beaten and painted and found the next morning by her father and sister.

accounts.label: Topeka Journal (via Wichita Eagle)
accounts.gist: Called the Kansas City Times account of the burning 'Another lie' and protested the circulation of 'lies about Kansas'.

framing.detail: Eastern and Southern dailies ran the merchant wire under headlines such as 'Thought She Was Hoodooed' and 'Superstition in the West'; the Memphis Appeal added 'A Pursuing Posse Will do Some Lynching.'
The Beatty version ran as 'Burned to Break a Spell' and 'A Fiend's Crime', calling the servant an 'old fiend' and speaking of an arrest rather than a lynching.
The Smyrna Times called the servant's belief 'crazy' and 'hoodoo rot' and predicted the lynching party would 'in all probability' succeed, without objecting to it.
The Topeka Journal, reprinted by the Wichita Eagle, condemned the story itself as a lie damaging to Kansas.
